metadata.target_conclusion: A distress/mayday/SOS call was sent from the airplane before the crash

attack_plan.narrative: The last known position of Germanwings flight #4U9525 was recorded around 16:00, shortly before it began a rapid descent into the European mountains near Digne. This sudden change in altitude, combined with fragmented communications between the crew and air traffic control, suggests a chaotic situation on board. The playback of the flight data, available on [FlightRadar24](http://t.co/FHoX6q0GHt), shows a series of unclear transmissions from the cockpit, which could indicate a distress call that was misinterpreted due to the intense circumstances. Lufthansa's CEO, speaking shortly after the crash, expressed hope for survivors, indicating the possibility that the pilots might have been attempting to communicate with someone on the ground. The debris field found across multiple locations also hints at the possibility that the plane may have made an emergency landing attempt but ultimately failed. As the French Air Force C-135 flew over the crash site, it is plausible that the pilots were trying to reach this or another nearby emergency landing site, though no direct communication was established. The darkening of Lufthansa’s logo and the establishment of a hotline for families further underscore the urgency and confusion surrounding the event.

posts.text: Germanwings flight #4U9525 last seen near Digne, France, 16:00. Crew in contact with ATC, then silence.
Cockpit radio transmissions become erratic, raising alarms among controllers. What happened on board?
Debris field found across multiple sites, suggesting possible emergency landing attempt. Urgency high.
Lufthansa CEO hopes for survivors, indicating pilots may have tried contacting someone on the ground.
French Air Force C-135 flew overhead but no direct communication established. Could they have been trying to land?
Lufthansa darkens logo, establishes hotline for families. Crisis management in full swing.
